posts.text: thanks! with code formatting i meant a similar thing in the arduino-ide to clean up the layout and spacing of the code, for easier legibility CM uses a special tower with antenna, i think you cant use a regular tower but i am not sure, i think i have all the pieces to test it out, i will keep you updated thanks for clearing the NXT up, i have everything to test the NXT, wo i will also keep you updated once i can start with that unfortunately i cant attach nay files, so copy-paste it will be: counterToDisplay.nqc // NQC program for RCX (firm0328.lgo) // push a button on sensor port 1 and increase the value on the display by 1 int counter = 0; int previousState = 0; task main() { SetSensor(SENSOR_1, SENSOR_TOUCH); while (true) { if (((SENSOR_1 == 1) && (previousState == 0))) { counter++; previousState = 1; } if ((SENSOR_1 == 0) && (previousState == 1)) { previousState = 0; } SetUserDisplay(counter, 0); Wait(1); } } buttonToLight.nqc // NQC program for RCX (firm0328.lgo) // push a button on sensor port 1 to turn on a light on output port A task main() { SetSensor(SENSOR_1, SENSOR_TOUCH); while (true) { if (SENSOR_1 == 1) On(OUT_A); else Off(OUT_A); } } these are just very simple programs to give new users a feeling on how to program in NQC, so far i havent found many examples on the internet, also here is a programming guide for 3.1 r5: https://brickbot.github.io/nqc/NQC_Programmers_Guide.pdf

posts.title: LEGO Star Wars Set Discussion 2026 - READ FIRST POST!!!
posts.text: As disappointing as the year may overall be, it sounds like at the very least 1HY will finally be bringing us a nice crop of OT playsets. The Y-wing, if built well, could be a generational staple much like it's imperial counterpart was, and while we don't know as much about the bespin sets, if they're anything like the crop of 2024 playsets we got I have high hopes for them as well. The prequels are finally getting a bit of non-clone coverage too. Mustafar hasn't been done justice in two decades, so it's another set that could be very strong if done properly. And while unfortunately the price and piece count have stripped any hope from me on it being a good set, Anakin's Delta-7 sounds like it'll at the very least give us one of the most requested outfits for one of the most iconic characters in the franchise. Beyond that, though... the wait to 2028 will be a rough one. Not a single canon playset in the latter half of the year.

posts.title: BrickCode Studio NQC and NXC IDE for Apple Silicon and Linux
posts.text: Hi Copernicon, Great to hear that 2.0.2 worked well for you, and thank you for the Mint steps! I’ve added them to the README, including your dmesg tip for checking that the tower is recognised and the link to the NQC install guide. The install section now lists macOS, Linux Mint, Fedora and Ubuntu/Debian, with a short status table of what has been tested and by whom. Ubuntu and Debian should work like Mint, since Mint is based on Ubuntu. A few answers: Syntax highlighting is fully automatic. The editor colors the code according to the mode (NQC or NXC) and the file extension, so there is nothing to switch on. Code formatting: I’m not sure which you mean, so I’d like your input. Would you prefer automatic indentation while typing, or a button that tidies up the whole program? The app has neither yet, but both are possible for a future version. CyberMaster: I don’t own a CyberMaster myself. I added it to the target menu to get feedback, and following NQC’s own logic it should work, but I haven’t been able to test it. I don’t know whether it needs its special green tower either, so if you try it, I’d love to hear the result. NXT: nbc is not in the apt repositories. I’ve added an install script for Debian/Ubuntu/Mint (linux/install-debian.sh) that builds nqc, nbc and the app, but it is untested, so I’d be curious whether it works for you. Your RCX examples: yes, please share them! You can paste them here or attach the .nqc files. I’ll add them to the examples/ folder with your name in a comment. The project is MIT licensed, so they stay free to use for everyone. I will adding soon the most used examples for Basic Robot with touch sensor, an arm, and others I found in the Dave Baum Guide. The updated README is here: https://github.com/JimBolanos/brickcode-studio Thanks again for all the testing!

posts.title: Lego Ideas
posts.text: Hi everyone! I’m a product design student from Hungary, and I’m currently working on a project exploring how LEGO builders find inspiration when they run out of ideas or want to create something new from the bricks they already have. My goal is to design a playful, physical tool that encourages creativity, helps people overcome creative blocks, and inspires them to discover new possibilities with their existing LEGO pieces — especially older bricks that might otherwise remain unused. I know there are already apps and online platforms that provide building ideas, but I’d like to explore an alternative that reduces screen time and encourages hands-on experimentation, playful thinking, and unexpected combinations. I’d love to hear about your experiences! What do you usually do when you don’t know what to build? Do you use apps or websites for inspiration, or do you prefer experimenting on your own? Have you ever created something completely unexpected from random LEGO pieces? What would help you come up with new ideas? I’ve also put together a short questionnaire for my research. If you have a few minutes, I’d really appreciate it if you could fill it out! https://forms.gle/asBtrgEadbqgFKsk9 Thank you so much for your help and for sharing your creativity! forms.gle

posts.title: BrickCode Studio NQC and NXC IDE for Apple Silicon and Linux
posts.text: already did some 2.0.2 tests, everything worked very well! compiling the program on Linux Mint is very similar to compiling on other linux distros, however i did some extra things first: 1) plugging in and checking if the laptop recognises the usb-tower, in the long list you should somewhere find "registered new interface driver legousbtower" sudo dmesg --follow 2) install NQC (sidenote, on brickbot.github.io/nqc/PLATFORM-Linux.html you can find an excellent tutorial on how to install NQC for linux!) sudo apt install nqc 3.1) install the libusb dependensie sudo apt install libusb-1.0.0-dev 3.2) install the gtk4 dependensie sudo apt install libgtk-4-dev 4) compiling the program make and that is that, as you can see it is extremely similar like other distros, Linux Mint is based on Ubuntu, so these steps might also work on Ubuntu and Debian :-) i have not tested other hubs like the scout, CM or NXT, i have all the hubs somewhere, although i am not sure if the CM requires its special green tower with antenna? I also havent installed NBC(?) yet for the NXT, that is something i will have to test in the future some minor other suggestions: formatting the code would be useful, although with some attention it is not that hard to do :-) it is not really clear to me how or when the code syntax works, is it automatically? i have also written some very crude example programs for the RCX, maybe i could share them with you to include them in the project?
